title_en: Homily Delivered in the Church of Cyrinus
author: Cyril of Alexandria
occasion: A homily delivered in the Church of Cyrinus on the thirteenth of the Egyptian month Phamenoth, introduced as interpreting the saying of Isaiah: 'Death swallowed and prevailed, and again God removed every tear from every face.'
argument: God, being life and life-giving, willed that humanity be an incorruptible living creature on earth, even though its nature is corruptible. An unnamed adversary, wicked and envious, plotted against the human race and opposed the Creator's will. He cunningly brought humanity down into disobedience, knowing that through disobedience humanity would fall into death. The extant excerpt does not contain the actual interpretation of the Isaiah quotation; it only presents the lemma and then moves to this narrative about God and the adversary.

cast.name: God
cast.who: The Creator of all things, who is life and life-giving.

cast.name: The adversary
cast.who: An unnamed wicked and envious figure who plots against humanity and opposes God's will; identified as the devil only by inference.

cast.name: Humanity
cast.who: The human race, created with a corruptible nature but intended by God for incorruption.

voices.speaker: Isaiah (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as the saying of Isaiah being interpreted: τὸ τοῦ Ἠσαΐου ῥητὸν... τὸ φάσκον

key_terms.sense: Life itself, a title for God as the source of all life.
Life-giving, describing God's active power to impart life.
Incorruptible, not subject to decay or death.
Corruptible, subject to decay and death, describing human nature.
Wicked, morally evil, describing the adversary.
Envious, begrudging, describing the adversary's attitude toward humanity.
Disobedience, the act by which humanity fell into death.
Death, the consequence of disobedience and the power Isaiah says was swallowed.

scripture: The homily quotes Isaiah in a form close to the Septuagint. Isaiah 25:8 in modern citation corresponds to the quoted text: 'Death swallowed and prevailed, and again God removed every tear from every face.'
uncertain: The exact date of the homily in the modern calendar

The full extent of the original homily, since the source appears to be an excerpt
Whether the unnamed adversary (ὁ δέ) is explicitly the devil; the text does not name him

_unresolved_facts.fix: The extant excerpt does not contain the actual interpretation of the Isaiah quotation beyond the narrative about God and the adversary; however, the source material is fragmentary and we cannot determine what originally followed.

_unresolved_facts.claim: The adversary ... identified as the devil only by inference.
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ὁ δέ, ἐπείπερ ἦν πονηρὸς καὶ βάσκανος, ἐπεβούλευσε τῷ γένει, ἀντετάττετο τῇ βουλήσει τοῦ δημιουργοῦ, κατεκόμισε πανούργως εἰς παρακοήν, εἰδὼς ὅτι πεσεῖται δι' αὐτῆς εἰς θάνατον.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The adversary is not identified as the devil at all in the extant text; the text uses ὁ δέ with no explicit identification, and any identification beyond 'wicked and envious adversary' goes beyond what the source supports.

_unresolved_facts.fix: A repetition of the title and incipit appears, cutting off at 'καὶ πάλιν' ('and again'). The source does not indicate whether this is due to damage, excerpting, or editorial practice.

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ἐν ᾗ τὸ τοῦ Ἠσαΐου ῥητὸν ἑρμηνεύει τὸ φάσκον· Κατέπιεν ὁ θάνατος ἰσχύσας καὶ πάλιν ἀφεῖλεν ὁ θεὸς πᾶν δάκρυον ἀπὸ παντὸς προσώπου.
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text of Isaiah is cited as a lemma to be interpreted (τὸ τοῦ Ἠσαΐου ῥητὸν ἑρμηνεύει), not presented as a direct voice or quotation marked with conventional speech markers; the 'speaker' is better described as 'Isaiah (text cited as lemma)'.
